facts.claim: Italy (our page): bomboniere are small gifts given to guests as thanks, often including sugared almonds; confetti in Italy means sugared almonds or small round sweets rather than paper. Read via Apify web-fetch.
Italy (our page): La Serenata is described as the groom serenading the bride-to-be beneath her window on the eve of the wedding, accompanied by musicians. Read via Apify web-fetch.
facts.conflicts: Our page gives no source. Re-sourcing from a reputable cultural source not completed in this batch; writer should present as 'a custom in parts of Italy' or link to our page rather than state history.

facts.claim: Our Italy page also states the veil 'is believed to ward off evil spirits', lists a 'unity tree' planting and 'La Festa della Taranta at midnight' as Italian wedding traditions. None is sourced on the page.
facts.conflicts: Do not repeat these in the pillar: the evil-spirits veil line conflicts with the brief's rule (folklore only as 'often said' with a reputable source); unity tree and midnight Taranta are unsourced. Flag for a later refresh of the Italy page.

facts.claim: Sulmona (Abruzzo) is widely described as the centre of Italian sugared-almond (confetti) making; a search summary of an Italian botanical heritage site says sugared almonds were used to celebrate births and weddings from Roman times.
facts.source: https://luoghi.italianbotanicalheritage.com/en/confetti-di-sulmona/ (search summary via Apify rag-web-browser; page not fully read)
facts.conflicts: Roman-origin claim is myth-prone and only from a secondary site. Use Sulmona as 'known for confetti' only after [[VERIFY]] against an official Abruzzo/Italian tourism source. The 'odd number of almonds' custom was not found in any source: omit.

facts.claim: UNESCO inscribed 'Henna: rituals, aesthetic and social practices' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2024 (19.COM, decision 7.b.15), nominated jointly by 16 Arab states: UAE, Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Mauritania, Morocco, Oman, State of Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Tunisia and Yemen.

UNESCO describes henna paste as commonly used by women for adornment (dyeing hair and fingertips, decorating hands and feet); it is a symbol of joy used on festive occasions such as births and weddings, and its use is often accompanied by chants, songs, proverbs and poems.
UNESCO's decision notes henna paste is given as a gift on occasions including weddings, and that henna rituals mark important life events and strengthen social bonds.

In inscribing henna, UNESCO's committee encouraged states to watch for the 'potential risk of decontextualization and over-commercialization of the element'. Useful framing for the brief's respect note on borrowing customs.

Britannica (mahr, marriage custom): in Muslim marriage the groom promises a mahr, a commitment to provide his bride with wealth in her lifetime (Britannica's India 'Family and kinship' article, linked from the mahr topic page). Read via Apify web-fetch.
facts.conflicts: The same Britannica topic page quotes its Yemen article describing mahr as 'bride-price, given by the father of the groom' in Yemen. Writer should use the general definition (a gift or commitment from the groom to the bride) and not the 'bride-price' wording.

facts.claim: Nikah (the marriage contract) and walima (the celebratory reception after it): no encyclopaedia definition was read in this batch. A search summary of Wikipedia's 'Marriage in Islam' says all Islamic marriage contracts include a mahr and that the nikah is typically followed by a reception (walima). Wikipedia is not an accepted source for the article.
facts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_in_Islam (search summary only, not an accepted source)
facts.conflicts: [[VERIFY]] nikah and walima definitions against Britannica or Oxford Reference before the writer uses them; or link to /guides/muslim-wedding-traditions and keep wording minimal.

facts.claim: Quaich: from the Gaelic 'cuach' (cup); a shallow bowl with two lug handles. Earliest examples were wooden; silver mounts were added from the mid-17th century and all-silver quaichs were made by the 1660s. The site cites National Museums Scotland ('Uniquely Scottish silver: top 5 highlights from the silver collections') and F. Marian McNeill, The Scots Kitchen (1929). Read via Apify rag-web-browser.
facts.conflicts: Secondary fact-checking site, not the museum itself. [[VERIFY]] the 1660s and Gaelic etymology lines against nms.ac.uk before stating dates.

facts.claim: Quaich myth-check: the popular story that two handles meant neither drinker could hold a weapon (and that the host drank first to prove no poison) has no early source; it is a modern explanation. Couples today share a quaich at Scottish weddings, usually with whisky.
facts.conflicts: Good candidate for the article's myth-versus-documented thread, but cite as 'often said' and hedge until NMS is checked.

facts.claim: San-san-kudo: a search summary of a Japan travel guide describes it as a Shinto wedding ritual in which the couple take turns sipping sake from three cups ('nuptial cups').
facts.source: https://www.japan-experience.com/plan-your-trip/to-know/understanding-japan/weddings (search summary via Apify rag-web-browser; page not fully read)
facts.conflicts: Travel-company source, below the brief's standard. [[VERIFY]] against a shrine, Kokugakuin Encyclopedia of Shinto or JNTO source; search for the Kokugakuin entry returned nothing usable this batch.

facts.claim: Lazo and arras: a search summary of a United States Conference of Catholic Bishops media blog post (Dec 2013) describes the lazo and veil and the giving of coins (arras) as customs popular at weddings in Latin America, with the lazo symbolising the new union.
facts.source: http://usccbmedia.blogspot.com/2013/12/hispanic-customs-of-lazo-veil-and-coins.html (search summary only; full page failed to load via Apify web-fetch)
facts.conflicts: Page not fully read. The '13 coins for Jesus and the 12 apostles' explanation appeared only in a Facebook answer (not a source): do not use it. [[VERIFY]] lazo/arras meaning and their Philippine use (e.g. National Commission for Culture and the Arts) before stating detail.

insider_details.detail: Henna nights are a living, UNESCO-recognised heritage across 16 Arab states, and UNESCO itself warns about decontextualisation and over-commercialisation; for couples outside that heritage, the respectful route is to be invited into a family's henna night, or have a local henna artist lead it with its songs, rather than staging it as a styling station.
In Italy, sugared almonds (confetti) do double duty: tossed or gifted on the day and packed into bomboniere as the guest thank-you, so they replace a separate favour at a destination wedding.

The quaich is one of the easiest customs to borrow: one shared cup, a short moment, and it suits a symbolic ceremony abroad; just tell guests the honest story (a Highland hospitality cup) rather than the weapons-and-poison legend, which has no early source.

Mahr is part of the Islamic marriage contract, not a reception flourish, so in a Muslim wedding abroad it is agreed within the nikah with the officiant and family; the planner's job is the timeline and space for the nikah and walima, not the content.

Shared-cup and binding rituals (san-san-kudo, lazo, quaich, stefana) sit inside specific faiths or ceremonies; for borrowing, ask the officiant or venue whether a symbolic version is welcome, and leave religious rites to couples of that faith.
